html:
When I first started guitar, I thought the F chord was humanly impossible; anyone who could hold it down was a god.

Once I could hold down the F chord, I thought anyone who could switch between chords without stumbling was a god.

Once I could switch chords, I thought anyone who could strum and sing at the same time was a god.

Once I could strum and sing Jay Chou’s “Sunny Day,” I discovered Sungha Jung… and decided fingerstyle players were gods.

I finally got all the way through “Nostalgia,” but it sounded awful. Why? Turns out you also need rhythm.

So on goes the metronome. My timing got better, but it still didn’t sound good. Turns out you also have to watch your dynamics and not just bash away at the strings from the first note.

Once I’d sorted out the dynamics, I needed emotion.

Then I discovered that beyond “Nostalgia” there were faster pieces, pieces at a similar tempo but in a different meter, pieces that break all the rules, pieces with stretches that pull your hand apart, chords you can’t hold down, percussive slaps on the strings, and retuning the pegs in the middle of a song. And on top of all these advanced techniques, you have to bring in rhythm, dynamics and emotion at the same time. Beyond that, there’s writing your own.

That’s where you see who really has it.

I don’t really play piano. The only thing standing between me and Lang Lang is Lang Lang.

But I’d guess the gap between one pianist and another is much like it is on the guitar.
